Yes. Feminizing GAHT-associated proteins strongly overlap with sex-associated proteins from the general-population Olink dataset.

Using adjusted p < 0.05 in either CPA-GAHT or SPIRO-GAHT, 299 of 5279 tested proteins were GAHT-associated. Of these, 259 overlapped the provided sex-associated protein set (86.6% of GAHT-associated proteins), far more than the 147.6 expected by chance given 2606 sex-associated proteins among 5279 tested proteins (one-sided hypergeometric/Fisher p = 4.11e-44, odds ratio = 7.26).

The overlap was present for both antiandrogen regimens: CPA-GAHT had 213/245 significant proteins overlapping the sex-associated set (86.9%; p = 9.23e-37), and SPIRO-GAHT had 81/91 overlapping (89.0%; p = 7.21e-16). Proteins significant in both regimens showed especially strong overlap (35/37; p = 3.02e-09).

Top overlapping examples included SPINT3, INSL3, EDDM3B, PROK1, PRL, TEX101, OMD, SPOCK1, VIT, and PLB1. Direction was often but not always concordant with the female-vs-male general-population estimate: among overlapping hits with non-missing sex beta, 110/173 CPA-significant proteins and 52/68 SPIRO-significant proteins had the same sign as the female-associated direction.

Conclusion: there is a strong and statistically enriched overlap, indicating that many proteins altered after feminizing GAHT are also proteins that differ by sex in the general population. The overlap is incomplete, so GAHT does not simply reproduce all general-population sex-associated proteomic differences, and the result should be interpreted as shared protein-level association rather than proof of identical mechanisms.
